lines.q1: Who decides how much money a country has? And if no new paper money is printed, how can there be so much more in the bank?
lines.c1: Cash is only a small slice. In most countries, roughly nine tenths of all money is just numbers in bank accounts.
lines.c2: Those numbers are real money. You can pay, save and borrow with them, exactly like cash.
lines.b1: So where does it come from? Mostly from banks. When a bank approves a loan, it types the amount into the borrower's account.
lines.b1b: That new deposit is new money, and no printing press is involved.
lines.b2: When the loan is repaid, the money disappears again. So the money supply grows and shrinks with lending.
lines.r1: Nobody controls it with a single switch. The central bank sets the interest rate, which is the price of borrowing. High rates mean fewer loans, and low rates mean more.
lines.r2: It also creates reserves, the money banks hold with it, and regulators set rules on how much banks may lend against their capital.
lines.r3: Governments matter too: when they spend and borrow, more money flows into accounts. And in the end, people and firms must want to borrow.
lines.i1: The real limit is not a number of notes. It is what the economy can produce. If money grows much faster than goods, prices rise, and that is inflation.
lines.outro: Money is mostly a promise, and managing it means managing trust.
